Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 11 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 441 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

Draft:

Students would benefit from being able to attend classes from home, as long as distance learning stays an option and does not become a requirement. Schools work well for most students, but not for all of them, and a flexible choice helps the ones who are left behind.

The strongest reason is access. Some students live far from school, and a long bus ride can eat two or three hours of a day. A student in a rural area could spend that time sleeping, studying, or finishing homework instead. Other students are sick for long stretches, recovering from surgery, or dealing with a chronic illness. Without distance learning, they fall behind or drop out. With it, they can keep up with the same lessons as their classmates and return to school without losing a year.

Distance learning also helps students who do not learn well in a crowded room. A shy student may be afraid to ask questions in front of thirty peers, but in a video class they can type a question in the chat. Students who are bullied might finally be able to focus on the lesson instead of worrying about the hallway. Some students also work at a different speed. When lessons are recorded, they can pause a difficult explanation and replay it as many times as they need.

Another benefit is flexibility for families. A teenager who helps care for a younger sibling, or who has a job to support the household, may find it nearly impossible to keep a strict schedule. Online classes let that student attend at hours that fit real life. Athletes and young performers who travel for competitions can stay enrolled without giving up their dreams.

Critics argue that students lose social contact and that many will not stay disciplined at home. These are fair concerns. A school is where friendships are made and where students learn to work with others. Some students will be tempted to watch videos or play games instead of listening. But these problems can be reduced. Schools can require regular check-ins, set clear attendance rules, and invite distance students to join clubs, labs, and special events in person. Students who show they cannot manage at home can be moved back to the classroom.

In the end, a school should serve the student, not the other way around. Because students have different needs, one setting will never be best for everyone. Offering distance learning as an option gives struggling, distant, ill, or overburdened students a real chance to succeed, while those who thrive in the classroom can stay there. That choice makes education fairer, and it is worth offering.
